title: POC: Autoscale / burst capacity & fallback planning - Orion Tech
customer_attendees: Meera Shah - Head of AI Product
summary: Redwood AE/SE scoped a two-week POC with Orion to validate capacity sizing and autoscale/burst behavior for a text-generation feature. Success criteria focus on p99 latency and cost per 1k tokens under a target, plus stable tail-latency during 10x traffic spikes. Workload profile and QPS distribution were collected; Redwood suggested a reserved pool (2 x A100-equivalent) with configured burst to 4 GPUs and fallback to smaller model + cached responses. Action items include sending benchmark template, proposed capacity numbers, and security docs. Agreed pilot window and next-runbook draft.
action_items: Maya Patel: Share benchmark template + model list (due 2025-09-04)
Ethan Morales: Produce initial capacity plan + cost estimate for reserved 2->4 GPU burst (due 2025-09-05)
Lena Park: Provide 7-day production QPS histogram and sample payloads (due 2025-09-04)
Greg Torres: Confirm VPC peering and KMS constraints and send network diagram (due 2025-09-08)
Meera Shah: Sign off on pilot success criteria doc (due 2025-09-09)
next_steps: Redwood to run initial micro-benchmarks with customer sample payloads
Schedule 1-hour runbook & canary run session in second week of POC
Exchange security questionnaire and SOC2 / ISO docs
Set pilot start date after we validate warmup / latency targets
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-02
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Morales (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Orion ML Platform Lead), Greg Torres (Orion Infra), Meera Shah (Orion Product)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on — quick intros, then we'll dive into the POC goals.
[00:10] Lena (Orion): Hi, thanks — I'm Lena, I run the ML infra team for Orion's conversational product.
[00:15] Greg (Orion): Greg here, infra. I'll be focused on networking and capacity allocation.
[00:20] Meera (Orion): Meera, product — I'll be tracking success criteria.
[00:25] Maya: Great. Ethan's our senior SE, he'll drive the technical portions.
[00:30] Ethan (Redwood SE): Morning all. Big picture: we want to size a reserved pool for your POC, define a burst strategy, and design fallbacks so customer-facing latency stays predictable during spikes.

[02:10] Lena: For context, our current traffic for the feature is around 12 QPS average with peaks up to 85 QPS during marketing bursts. Payloads vary; typical prompt is 400-800 tokens, but we have a tail up to 1,500 tokens. We're especially worried about tail latency.

[03:05] Ethan: Ok that helps. Can you confirm the SLA you want for the POC — e.g., p99 target?
[03:12] Meera: We want p99 < 800ms for 512-token responses and p95 < 300ms ideally. Cost target is a soft constraint: keep cost-per-1k tokens under $0.60 during normal load.
[03:30] Maya: Those are reasonable as POC goals. We'll validate with benchmarks. Two levers: reserved GPUs for base load and autoscale/burst for spiky traffic. We should also plan fallback behaviors if the burst pool is saturated.

[05:00] Greg: On infra side we'll only allow limited burst capacity due to budget. We can commit to 2 reserved GPUs for the POC but need to see numbers for when to trigger burst to 4 GPUs and what the cost delta would be.

[06:10] Ethan: Good. Based on early numbers, for your request profile (median 400–800 tokens, 12 QPS baseline) we'd propose a reserved pool equivalent to 2 x A100-80GB handles baseline with batching and prefix caching. Burst to 4 GPUs allows headroom for ~2.5x concurrent requests with acceptable tail behavior.

[07:05] Lena: What about warm caches — KV cache and prefix cache — how long to warm and how much do they help p99?
[07:15] Ethan: Two parts: warm KV cache with traffic patterns during canary will reduce repeated prefix costs; prefix/KV caching can drop token compute by ~30–60% for repeated prompts. Warmup depends on reuse — can be minutes to hours. We'll run micro-benchmarks with your sample prompts to estimate.

[08:45] Maya: Important operational detail: autoscale should prefer vertical fallback before rejecting. We recommend policy order: 1) route to compatible model variant (quantized or smaller), 2) use cached or approximate response, 3) queue with a short backoff for low-priority requests, 4) last resort reject with graceful degradation message.

[10:20] Greg: Smaller model fallback sounds fine but we need to understand delta in quality — Meera will weigh in. Also network egress for a cross-region fallback is a no-go for us. Must stay in same VPC/region.

[11:05] Meera: For product, we accept small quality drops for system messages but not for high-value user completions. Success criteria should encode quality thresholds on a small eval set.

[12:30] Ethan: Agreed. POC success criteria we propose: (a) p99 latency for 512 tokens < 800ms under baseline and under 10x synthetic spikes not exceeding 2x reserved capacity; (b) tail-latency degradation less than 2x from baseline; (c) quantifiable quality delta when falling back to a smaller model < 3% on your eval metrics; (d) cost-per-1k tokens under $0.60 on average.

[14:00] Lena: How will you run the 10x traffic test without impacting prod? We want a staged canary to avoid noisy neighbor issues.

[14:20] Ethan: We'll run load from a Redwood sandbox in your region, with traffic marked as test. We'll also schedule the run during your maintenance window. We'll simulate ramp up and validate autoscale triggers, burst provisioning times (time-to-ready), and fallback activation points.

[16:00] Maya: On timescales, recommended POC: two weeks. Week 1: data & micro-benchmarks, warmup, iterate capacity plan. Week 2: run ramp tests, canary, and evaluate success criteria with your eval set.

[17:00] Greg: What about burst spin-up time? If it takes 2–3 minutes to provision a GPU, that's not acceptable for user-facing bursts.

[17:20] Ethan: Good point. Our recommended approach uses a small warm standby pool (hot pool) plus instant fallback policies. Provisioning from 2->4 reserved may take ~90–180 seconds cold; with a warm pool of 1 hot instance you can reduce impact. We also recommend keeping quantized model variants preloaded for faster startup.

[19:10] Meera: So operationally we'd do reserved 2 GPUs + 1 hot standby (warm) and allow burst to leverage ephemeral GPUs up to 4 for short periods?

[19:30] Maya: Yes. That balances cost and tail control. We'll show cost numbers for 2 reserved + 1 hot standby vs just 2 reserved. The hot standby costs less than a full extra reserved since it's right-sized.

[20:50] Lena: Can you explain the fallback policy in more detail — what triggers model switch vs queued backoff?

[21:00] Ethan: Triggers are policy-based: threshold on queue length, observed p95/p99 crossing SLO for a sustained window (say 30s), and an observed drop in token throughput. Sequence: 1) if p95>target for 30s, start routing low-priority requests to smaller model; 2) if queue length exceeds 200 requests, enable short backoff queue for non-critical calls; 3) if all else fails, return cached/approx response for requests that match previous patterns.

[23:00] Speaker 1: there's a note here — caching is only effective if prompt variance is limited, right?
[23:08] Ethan: Correct, cache hit rate correlates with prompt reuse. For chat sessions with system prompts and repeated patterns we see big wins.

[24:20] Greg: Security — we need VPC peering, no egress, and KMS integration for keys. Can Redwood run in our VPC or do you need a private deployment?

[24:35] Maya: For POC we can run Redwood Private in your VPC (customer-managed control plane) or a hosted VPC peering depending on your compliance. For quick start we'll offer a managed VPC peering that keeps data in-region; if you need complete isolation we can option the Private package. We'll send the security questionnaire and SOC2 artifacts.

[26:10] Meera: Great. Also want to measure quality changes for fallback automatically. Can Redwood produce evaluation diffs for the POC?

[26:20] Ethan: Yes, we'll run automated evals on a holdout set across model variants during the POC and produce regression alerts. We'll include prompts and scoring metrics.

[28:00] Lena: About cost modeling — how do you model cost for bursts? We need to justify budget for ephemeral GPUs during high-traffic events.

[28:10] Maya: We'll provide an estimated cost-per-minute for reserved and burst instances, and an expected monthly delta given your 7-day traffic histogram. For example, if bursts are rare (2–3 times/month lasting <10 minutes) the incremental cost is small vs keeping higher reserved capacity. We'll send an Excel with scenarios.

[30:00] Ethan: Benchmarks we'll run: 1) single-request latency (median/p95/p99) for 512/1024/1500 tokens; 2) sustained throughput test to find saturation point with and without batching; 3) burst ramp test (1x -> 10x) to measure spin-up, failover, and fallback behavior; 4) cache-hit simulations.

[32:10] Meera: On success criteria for quality, we expect <3% delta on our Rouge/F1 style metric for the smaller quantized model. If delta is larger, fallback route should be disabled for those endpoints.

[33:40] Lena: We'll provide three representative workloads: short chat replies (~200 tokens), long explanatory (~900 tokens), and extended completion (~1500 tokens). We'll attach a sample of 200 prompts.

[35:05] Maya: Perfect. That sample will let us estimate effective batch sizes and token distribution. We'll instrument per-route dashboards to show token cost and latency.

[36:30] Greg: Networking again — we must avoid any cross-az egress for heavy payloads. If Redwood plans to use ephemeral GPUs in another AZ, that will hurt latency and costs.

[36:50] Ethan: Understood. We'll ensure burst capacity is in the same AZ/region and won't cross AZ boundaries unless configured. We'll note that in the runbook.

[38:15] Speaker 2: can we talk about model variants and quantization?
[38:20] Ethan: Sure. We'll propose: primary model (FP16 or bfloat16) for quality, and a quantized int8 variant as fallback. In the POC we'll test both for latency and a small eval set to measure quality difference. Quantized models load faster and use less memory so they help in constrained burst scenarios.

[40:00] Meera: Would you recommend always pre-loading quantized variant?
[40:05] Ethan: Yes, if memory allows. Preloading is a cheap win for fast fallback. If memory is tight, keep the quantized model in the warm pool rather than fully preloaded.

[41:30] Lena: How will we know when to increase reserved vs rely on burst? We want clear decision criteria after the POC.

[41:45] Maya: We'll include a decision matrix: if sustained utilization > 75% for a week and p99 breaches happen, recommend increasing reserved capacity. If bursts are frequent but short and costs low, keep reserved and rely on burst. We'll quantify thresholds in the final report.

[43:10] Greg: Operational runbook — I want explicit steps for autoscale failures and rollback.

[43:20] Ethan: We'll draft runbook actions: how to find the logs, how to force route traffic, how to promote a hot standby to reserved, and rollback steps for a model rollback. We'll demo the runbook during a 1-hour session in week 2.

[45:00] Meera: Anything we should be careful about in the POC?

[45:07] Maya: Two cautions: 1) synthetic traffic not representative of user diversity can overestimate cache hit rates; 2) cross-tenant noisy neighbor when sharing infra — so isolate the POC environment.

[46:30] Lena: We can provide production-like traffic for the micro-benchmarks. We'll anonymize payloads but keep distribution.

[47:15] Ethan: Good. We'll provide a small load generator script and a config to replay your histogram.

[48:40] Speaker 1: there's a comment about telemetry — do you expose per-token tracing for debugging?

[48:45] Ethan: Yes, per-request traces with token-level timing are available in the console (configurable retention). We'll include tracing hooks and a sample dashboard.

[50:00] Maya: Quick recap from Redwood: we'll produce a capacity plan, benchmark plan, cost scenarios, and security docs. We'll aim to start bench week on 2025-09-08 assuming we get sample payloads by 2025-09-04.

[50:20] Meera: That timeline works, tentative pilot start of 2025-09-15.

[51:40] Greg: I'll send network diagram and constraints by 2025-09-08.

[52:20] Lena: I'll upload 7-day QPS histogram and 200 sample prompts by Friday.

[53:00] Maya: Action items noted. Any outstanding questions?

[54:10] Meera: One question — competitors: we previously bench'ed Bedrock and Vertex; what would you say is Redwood's differentiation for autoscale?

[54:30] Maya: Short answer: we focus on production economics — smarter batching/caching and tiered fallbacks built into the serving runtime so autoscale + cost controls are integrated rather than bolted on. Also first-class private/VPC options for enterprise constraints.

[56:00] Speaker 3: brief crosstalk — okay thanks.

[56:30] Maya: Ok we'll wrap. Next steps: share docs, schedule week-2 runbook, and confirm pilot start date once we get artifacts.

[57:00] Meera: Thanks everyone.
[57:05] Lena: Thanks.
[57:07] Greg: Thanks all.
[57:10] Ethan: Thanks, talk soon.

[64:40] End of recording.
